headline: Canada, Philippines finish trade talks; U.S. flights still recovering
briefing: Prime Minister Carney and Philippine President Marcos announced Saturday that free-trade negotiations are complete, with a signing targeted for 2027; nothing changes at the border yet. Airlines are still clearing the backlog from Friday's four-hour halt to all U.S. departures, so check any cross-border flight from Pearson or Billy Bishop before leaving home. The White House says Trump will meet Putin and Xi together in China next week, and Canada's inflation report arrives Monday.

keyDates.label: ASEAN summit opens; new municipal term
keyDates.why: The Southeast Asian summit Carney is attending opens in Manila, Israel's security cabinet meets, and Ontario councils and the appointed regional chairs begin their four-year term.

keyDates.label: Canada inflation report; OSAP bill expected
keyDates.why: Statistics Canada reports October consumer prices, the last reading before the Bank of Canada's next decision, and Ontario is expected to table its bill on student aid at private career colleges.

keyDates.label: APEC summit; Alaska ranked-choice count
keyDates.why: Leaders meet in Shenzhen on Nov. 18–19, where Carney is to see Xi and the White House says Trump will meet Putin and Xi together; Alaska also tabulates its Peltola–Sullivan Senate race.

keyDates.label: Senate Democrats vote; Stelco recall
keyDates.why: Democratic senators choose between Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen for majority leader by secret ballot, and 175 laid-off Stelco workers are due back in Hamilton.

keyDates.label: Bank of Canada and Fed rate decisions
keyDates.why: Both central banks decide the same day; high U.S. wholesale inflation and Monday's Canadian report will shape whether rates rise again.

keyDates.label: Lutnick testifies
keyDates.why: The U.S. commerce secretary is due before the Senate Banking Committee over delayed export restrictions in the Nvidia chip scandal.

stories.headline: U.S. flights still recovering after FAA ground stop; Pearson lost more than 120 cross-border flights
stories.summary: Airlines are spending Saturday clearing the backlog from Friday's nationwide halt to U.S. departures, which the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered after a communications failure at its regional air traffic control centres. Toronto Pearson is in recovery mode, with more cancellations and delays possible through the weekend.
stories.now: The FAA ordered the stop at 3:54 p.m. Eastern on Friday and lifted it at 8:15 p.m., a halt of more than four hours. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed old equipment that became overloaded and asked Congress for billions of dollars more to modernize air traffic control; Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no sign of a cyberattack, though the investigation continues. Cancellation counts from the tracking site FlightAware climbed through the night and differ by outlet, from more than 4,700 to over 7,700 for Friday, with more than 2,000 Saturday flights reported cancelled; some Saturday departures from Paris and Frankfurt were also affected. Pearson's website showed more than 120 U.S. departures and arrivals cancelled on Friday plus about 20 other international flights, and Air Canada and Porter scrubbed their remaining Friday U.S. flights at Billy Bishop. Nav Canada, which runs Canadian air traffic control, said its own systems were normal but that delays may continue while the backlog clears, and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries called the failure an unprecedented breakdown.
stories.backstory: A ground stop is an order that keeps aircraft from taking off; planes already in the air continue to their destinations. Nationwide stops are very rare: CTV reported that Friday's was only the second halt of all U.S. departures since the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks, the other being a January 2023 failure of a pilot-notification system. The FAA's telecommunications network has caused regional stoppages before, including one in the Minneapolis area in August. Canada's own air traffic system was not affected, and the Greater Toronto Airports Authority said Pearson's systems were working normally. The outage came a day after an unrelated Microsoft email failure, and officials have not linked the two.

timeline.event: A notice-system outage causes the first nationwide U.S. ground stop since 2001
Telecommunications problem halts Minneapolis-area flights for about 90 minutes
FAA stops all U.S. departures at 3:54 p.m. Eastern; Pearson and Billy Bishop lose their cross-border flights
Order lifted at 8:15 p.m.; Duffy blames overloaded equipment and asks Congress for funding
Airlines work through the backlog; more than 2,000 Saturday flights reported cancelled

stories.why: A single network fault stopped departures across the world's busiest aviation system for hours, which raises questions about the age and resilience of U.S. air traffic control equipment. The administration is using it to press Congress for modernization money, while Democrats want a fuller account of what failed.
stories.impact: If you are flying between the GTA and the U.S. this weekend, check your flight with the airline before leaving for Pearson or Billy Bishop, because cancellations and delays are expected to linger. Air Canada has also warned that flights to the Caribbean and South America that cross U.S. airspace could be affected. Under Canada's air passenger rules, airlines must rebook you or refund you when a flight is cancelled, though cash compensation generally does not apply to disruptions outside the airline's control.

stories.backstory: Canada and the Philippines first discussed a trade agreement in 2015, and Carney and Marcos agreed in October 2025 to restart and speed up the talks, alongside a separate Canada-ASEAN negotiation. The push is part of Ottawa's effort to find customers beyond the United States as tariffs from the Trump administration hit Canadian exports. The Asia trip also takes Carney to China, where he has said he will raise foreign interference with Xi; a federal public inquiry found China was the most active foreign state trying to interfere in Canadian democratic institutions. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has criticized the travel, saying the economy is about people struggling to make ends meet rather than summits.
stories.headline: Canada and the Philippines finish free-trade talks; signing targeted for 2027
stories.impact: Nothing changes at the border yet, so prices and tariffs stay as they are until the agreement is signed and ratified, likely not before 2027. The Philippines is one of the largest sources of new immigrants to the GTA, so lower barriers could eventually matter for local importers, food businesses and Ontario exporters, including pork producers.
stories.now: The two countries' trade ministers signed a joint statement closing the negotiations while Carney and Marcos looked on, about a year after the talks were restarted. Carney said the deal could help triple two-way trade to more than $10 billion a year by 2035, from about $2.4 billion in 2025, and that both governments will move quickly to sign it and bring it into force in 2027. The text has not been released, and the Globe and Mail reported there was no word on whether Canada will be exempted from temporary limits on pork imports that Manila is bringing in this month; Canada sold about $279 million of pork products to the Philippines in 2024. On the broader agreement with the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the Prime Minister's Office says negotiations are substantially concluded and a Philippine official said they had wrapped up, while other reports note it has not been finalized. The ASEAN summit opens Sunday; Carney then goes to the Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh and to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' meeting in Shenzhen on Nov. 18–19, where he is to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Globe and Mail: Carney wraps up negotiations on trade deal with Philippines

stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. announced in Manila on Saturday that negotiations on a Canada-Philippines free trade agreement are complete, with both sides aiming to sign it next year. Ottawa also says talks on a wider deal with the Southeast Asian bloc are substantially concluded, though that agreement is not yet final.

timeline.event: Carney and Marcos agree to restart and speed up trade talks
The two leaders pledge in Vancouver to finish negotiations by year-end
Carney meets European leaders in Dublin, then leaves for Asia

APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen, where Carney is to meet Xi
Target for signing the Canada-Philippines agreement

stories.why: It is the first concrete result of a trip meant to show Canada can rely less on the United States for trade. Concluding talks is not the same as a deal in force: the agreement still has to be signed and ratified, and its tariff schedule has not been published.

stories.backstory: The Brampton plant built Dodge and Chrysler cars and has been idle for about three years while workers stayed on paid layoff. In May 2022 Ottawa agreed to give Stellantis $529 million to retool its Brampton and Windsor plants, and the company had planned to build the Jeep Compass in Brampton. In October 2025 it moved that vehicle to Illinois as U.S. tariffs on Canadian-made cars took hold. Stellantis signed a memorandum of understanding with Roshel in September, Unifor's contract expired Sept. 20, and the union declared an impasse over the plant's future.
stories.headline: Ottawa and Ontario pitch Stellantis an 'aggressive package' to stop Brampton sale
stories.impact: Thousands of Peel Region families depend on the plant and its parts suppliers, and most laid-off workers have no guarantee of a job with the new owner. Taxpayers have a stake on both sides: any new support package would be public money, and the gap between the $24 million Stellantis has offered and what Ottawa says it is owed may end up in court.
stories.now: Joly said Friday that Ottawa is still trying to find a way to prevent the sale to armoured-vehicle maker Roshel, working with Ontario and with Unifor, the union for more than 9,000 Stellantis workers in Canada; she described the offer as an aggressive package but gave no details of what is in it. Ontario Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli said the aim of meeting Filosa is to buy some time by getting the company to slow the sale down, and that the province has not advanced any money for Brampton so far; he said any support for the scenarios Unifor has proposed would come from Ontario's existing $2.5-billion auto support fund. The meeting follows Thursday's session with Stellantis Canada chief Trevor Longley; no date has been announced. Joly has said Ottawa cannot block the sale under the Investment Canada Act because the seller is a Canadian subsidiary, so its leverage is the subsidy agreement: up to $529 million was committed in 2022 for the Brampton and Windsor plants, and Stellantis has offered to return $24 million. Unifor president Lana Payne said the union did not hear the company commit to reversing course. The 30-day default period began Thursday, and Stellantis expects the sale to close by the end of the year.

Both governments plan to take the pitch to global chief executive Antonio Filosa.

stories.why: The sale ends hopes that a major GTA auto plant would restart vehicle production, and it tests whether governments can enforce the conditions attached to public subsidies. It also shows how U.S. tariffs are pulling auto investment out of Ontario.

stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, and Iran choked traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, route for about a fifth of the world's oil. A June peace memorandum briefly reopened it but collapsed in July, and the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping. Qatar gave Iran a new draft deal on Oct. 25. Trump has said the war will end soon, one way or the other.
stories.headline: Iran reports three tankers ablaze after hitting mines; Trump to raise the war with Putin and Xi
stories.impact: Lower crude usually reaches GTA gas pumps within days, and this month's drop has eased fuel and delivery costs. With talks stalled, tankers reportedly hitting mines and Israel's cabinet meeting Sunday, that relief could reverse when markets reopen Monday.
stories.now: A Revolutionary Guards statement carried by Iranian state media said two tankers, one of them a supertanker, exploded and burned after hitting a mine while trying to cross the strait on an unapproved route with their tracking systems off; a separate navy statement described a third tanker hit east of the strait. None of the ships was named and the reports have not been independently confirmed; the U.S. military says it has cleared the main shipping lanes, and Trump has accused Iran of inventing such incidents to push up energy prices. The White House said Friday that Trump intends to raise the war when he meets Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping in Shenzhen next week. Iranian official Mohsen Rezaei said no enriched nuclear material will leave the country and warned that a new U.S. attack would be answered with strikes on American bases, while the UN's International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) is pressing for access it says it needs to verify Iran's nuclear material. One market report put Brent's Friday settlement at US$95.84 and U.S. benchmark WTI (West Texas Intermediate) at US$88.56; markets are closed for the weekend, and Israel's security cabinet is due to meet Sunday.

stories.summary: Iran's navy and Revolutionary Guards said three oil tankers caught fire after striking mines in and near the Strait of Hormuz, claims the United States has consistently rejected. The White House said President Trump will bring up the Iran war at a planned meeting with the leaders of Russia and China next week; oil ended Friday near US$96 a barrel, down about 2.5% on the week.

stories.why: Oil prices are the main driver of higher inflation in Canada and the U.S.; the October spike is why the Bank of Canada raised rates on Oct. 28.

stories.headline: White House says Trump will meet Putin and Xi together in China next week
stories.summary: The White House said Friday that President Trump will hold a joint meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, described as the first three-way sit-down between leaders of the three countries. It is planned for the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen and is to focus on limiting nuclear weapons.
stories.now: According to the White House, the meeting will take place around the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' summit in Shenzhen, which runs Nov. 18–19; no exact date or time was given. The stated focus is nuclear non-proliferation, meaning efforts to limit the spread and build-up of nuclear weapons, and U.S. officials played down the chance of a new agreement, calling the talks a starting point. Trump also plans to raise the Iran war but, per U.S. reports, not the war in Ukraine in that setting, and he is scheduled to meet Xi separately. Beijing and Moscow had not officially confirmed taking part as of the latest reports. Prime Minister Mark Carney will be at the same summit and is due to meet Xi.
stories.backstory: New START, the last treaty capping U.S. and Russian nuclear arsenals, expired in February 2026 with no replacement. Trump has said for some time that he wants three-way arms talks that include China, which has a smaller but growing arsenal and has been reluctant to join. The announcement comes after Republican losses in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, during stalled U.S.-led talks on Ukraine and amid tension with China over the Nvidia chip-export scandal. Trump and Xi last met in person in October 2025.

timeline.event: Trump and Xi meet in person in South Korea

stories.why: The three countries hold nearly all of the world's nuclear weapons and there is currently no treaty limiting them. A joint meeting would also be a notable moment for Putin, whom Western governments have tried to isolate since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
stories.impact: There is no direct effect on daily life in Ontario. The meeting matters here mainly through what follows from it: any easing or worsening of the Iran war moves gas prices, and U.S.-China relations shape the trade pressure Canada faces from both.

stories.backstory: Wholesale prices often signal where consumer prices are heading a few months later. Oil surged after the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, with Brent crude peaking above US$117 in late October, and tariffs have added to import costs. The Federal Reserve held its rate on Oct. 28, the same day the Bank of Canada raised its policy rate to 2.5%, its first increase in more than three years. Canada's annual inflation rate was 3.1% in September.
stories.headline: U.S. wholesale inflation hits 6.5%; stocks slip Friday but end the week higher
stories.impact: If you are renewing a mortgage or carrying a variable-rate loan in Ontario, higher U.S. rates raise the odds of higher borrowing costs here. Rising U.S. wholesale food prices can also feed into grocery bills, since Ontario imports much of its fresh produce from the U.S.
stories.now: The U.S. producer price index, which tracks what businesses receive for goods and services before they reach shoppers, rose 0.3% in October, a little under the 0.4% economists expected; the 6.5% annual rate compared with a 6.6% forecast. Leaving out food and energy, prices were up 0.3% on the month and 5% on the year, and wholesale food prices jumped 1.3%, the most since February. At Friday's close the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.1% at about 52,347, the S&P 500 down 0.4% at 7,561.67 and the Nasdaq down 0.9% at 25,136.27, with chipmakers leading the declines, according to Yahoo Finance and the Associated Press; for the week the S&P 500 gained about 2.5%, the Nasdaq 2.3% and the Dow 2.1%. In Toronto, the S&P/TSX Composite Index slipped 0.09% to 36,105.90 and was up about 0.9% on the week. U.S. coverage says the data keeps the Federal Reserve on course to raise interest rates in December, and one market report put the odds of a Bank of Canada increase that month at about 64%.

Yahoo Finance: Dow rises, S&P 500 and Nasdaq slip to cap volatile week

stories.summary: Prices charged by U.S. producers rose 0.3% in October and 6.5% from a year earlier, the biggest annual increase since November 2022. The S&P 500 fell 0.4% and the Nasdaq 0.9% on Friday, though all three main U.S. indexes still gained more than 2% on the week.

stories.why: Persistent price pressure in the United States makes further interest-rate increases there more likely. Canadian bond yields and mortgage rates tend to follow U.S. ones, and the Bank of Canada decides on the same day as the Fed, Dec. 9.

stories.backstory: Oil prices jumped after the U.S.-Iran war disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz this year, and fuel costs have pushed up inflation since. Canada's annual rate rose to 3.1% in September, led by gasoline, while core measures stayed near 2%. On Oct. 28 the Bank of Canada raised its policy rate to 2.5%, its first increase in more than three years, and said more hikes were possible. Oil has since fallen from a late-October peak above US$117 to the mid-US$90s.
stories.headline: Canada's October inflation report lands Monday, with forecasts from 3.0% to 3.3%
stories.impact: If you have a variable-rate mortgage or line of credit, or are renewing soon, this report will shape what happens to your payments in December. It will also show whether October's fuel spike reached grocery and other prices in Ontario.
stories.now: A Reuters poll of economists points to 3.2%, up from 3.1% in September. RBC expects a slight easing to 3.0%, with core inflation, which strips out volatile items, slipping to 1.9% from 2.1%; Continuum Economics forecasts 3.3%, which would be the highest since December 2023. Desjardins economist LJ Valencia expects a reading similar to or slightly above September's. CIBC's Avery Shenfeld and Helen Lao argue inflation will not climb as much as the Bank of Canada projects, which would leave less need for more rate increases. The central bank has said it expects inflation to stay above 3% through much of 2027, and one market report Friday put the odds of a December hike at about 64%.

stories.summary: Statistics Canada reports October consumer prices on Monday, the last inflation reading before the Bank of Canada's Dec. 9 rate decision. Economists expect the annual rate to stay close to September's 3.1%, but disagree on whether high energy costs are spreading to other prices.

stories.why: Monday's number is the main piece of evidence the Bank of Canada will have before deciding whether to raise rates again. A reading above 3.2% with firmer core prices would strengthen the case for a hike.

stories.backstory: Huang co-founded Nvidia and has run it since 1993, building it into the main supplier of the chips used to train artificial intelligence (AI) systems and one of the world's most valuable companies. Earlier this week, reports said the company had opened an internal investigation into whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort through a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly passed information to Beijing. Huang told staff in a company email that he had been unfaithful in his marriage. The stock had already slipped on that first report before Wednesday's news.
stories.headline: Trump advisers discuss Lutnick's future as Nvidia chip scandal reaches cabinet
stories.impact: Most Canadian pension plans, index funds and RRSP or TFSA portfolios that track U.S. stocks hold Nvidia, so its swings show up in retirement savings here. The company's next results and its CEO search could bring more volatility.
stories.now: Bessent told CNBC that Treasury, the State and Defense departments and the U.S. Trade Representative had for months favoured adding Megaspeed International to an export-control list, but that Commerce is in charge of that decision. CNN reported Friday that Trump advisers have discussed whether Lutnick should go and that the president has taken calls from officials and outside allies raising concerns; CNBC reported that Trump is standing by him for now. CNBC also reported that Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm Lutnick used to lead and that his sons now run, has business ties to Nvidia, which an ethics expert said raises questions. Reuters has reported that Megaspeed bought more than US$4.8 billion of Nvidia's advanced chips since June 2024; the company denies wrongdoing, and the Commerce Department denies an Axios account of a Situation Room confrontation between the two secretaries. Republican Sen. John Kennedy wants to know why the sales were approved, and Huang has agreed to testify to a House committee in a closed session by U.S. Thanksgiving (Nov. 26). Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10. Chief financial officer Colette Kress remains interim chief executive while the board searches for a successor.

sources.title: CNN: Bessent points finger at Commerce as Trump advisers discuss possible Lutnick ouster
CNBC: Lutnick faces questions over Nvidia scandal; sons' firm has ties to the chipmaker

stories.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly blamed the Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for being slow to restrict Nvidia chip sales to a Singapore-based firm suspected of supplying China, and CNN reported that some of President Trump's advisers have discussed removing Lutnick. Nvidia shares fell about 2.4% on Friday, a day after co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive.

stories.why: Nvidia is central to the artificial intelligence (AI) boom and one of the largest stocks in major U.S. indexes, and it has never had another chief executive. The spying allegation also raises national-security questions in Washington, which controls what chips the company may sell to China.

stories.backstory: Cleveland-Cliffs bought Stelco in 2024 and made job and investment commitments as part of Ottawa's approval of the takeover. Layoff notices this fall prompted Prime Minister Carney to accuse the company of betraying workers, and Ottawa threatened court action under the Investment Canada Act, the law that governs foreign takeovers. The company's chief executive called the federal threats bullying. U.S. tariffs on steel have squeezed Canadian mills that sell into the American market.
stories.headline: Stelco to recall 175 laid-off Hamilton workers on Dec. 1, with back pay
stories.impact: For Hamilton-area steelworkers and the suppliers that depend on them, it means paycheques resume before the holidays. It also signals to other Ontario employers with federal commitments that Ottawa is willing to escalate.
stories.now: The company said it has lined up enough customer commitments to restart the idled cold-rolled and coated steel lines, and that Stelco will make up the regular pay workers missed while they were off the job. When the cuts were announced this fall, Stelco said up to 500 workers could be affected and blamed U.S. tariffs, weak demand for Canadian steel and competition from imports; on Friday it put the number actually affected at 175. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly had refused to meet the company's leadership until workers were recalled and last week asked the Competition Bureau to examine its conduct. Ottawa says Cleveland-Cliffs agreed to keep unionized employment at 2024 levels through 2029; the company has denied breaking its commitments under the Investment Canada Act. Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, said it should never have come to this.

stories.summary: Cleveland-Cliffs, the U.S. owner of Stelco, said Friday it will restart finishing operations at the Hamilton plant and bring back all 175 affected employees on Dec. 1. The reversal follows weeks of pressure from Ottawa, which said the layoffs broke promises made when the company bought Stelco.

stories.why: It is a rare case of a foreign owner backing down after Ottawa pressed it over promises made at takeover. It comes the same week the federal government is using a similar approach with Stellantis over the Brampton plant.

stories.backstory: Republicans have held both chambers since January 2025, and all 435 House seats and about a third of the Senate were on the ballot. More than 53 million Americans voted early. Tariffs and high gas prices tied to the Iran war weighed on Trump's approval, and recent polls gave Democrats an edge in most key Senate races. Courts also turned back a Trump administration bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots.
stories.headline: Democrat Kreiss-Tomkins wins Alaska governorship; Senate race there still uncalled
stories.impact: Canadian exporters are watching whether a Democratic Congress moves to limit tariffs, which could ease pressure on Ontario manufacturers over time; near-term tariffs stay in place unless the White House changes them.
stories.now: NPR reported the Alaska result overnight, and The Hill said Decision Desk HQ projects Kreiss-Tomkins as the first Democrat to win the governor's office there in more than 20 years; a 37-year-old former state legislator who campaigned on bipartisanship, he would be the youngest governor in Alaska's history. Holscher, a state senator, beat Masterson, who had Trump's endorsement, in what local media call the closest Kansas governor's race in more than 50 years; station KSN reported her lead grew past 7,000 votes once late-arriving ballots were counted. The result keeps the governor's office in Democratic hands. Trump on Thursday praised Colom for campaigning among his supporters in the final days of the race. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith conceded to Colom on Wednesday; he is the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since 1982 and will be the state's first Black senator since the Reconstruction era after the Civil War. Mississippi counties must send official results to the secretary of state by Friday. Alaska is the last uncalled Senate race: Democrat Mary Peltola's lead over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan narrowed to 3,975 first-choice votes after Wednesday's count, The Hill reported, with Peltola a little under 49% and Sullivan about 47%; the ranked-choice tabulation is set for Nov. 18.

stories.summary: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins was declared the winner of the Alaska governor's race, taking an office Republicans have held, days after Democrats won the Kansas governorship and a Mississippi Senate seat. Alaska's Senate contest between Democrat Mary Peltola and Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is the last one uncalled.

stories.why: Colom's win in a state Republicans had held for more than four decades pads the Senate majority Democrats take over in January. A bigger majority makes it easier for them to block nominees, run investigations and force votes on tariffs.

stories.backstory: Many hospitals, universities, governments and businesses rent email and office software from Microsoft as an online service, known as Microsoft 365, rather than running their own servers. That means a single fault at the company can hit thousands of organizations at once. In July 2024 a faulty update from security firm CrowdStrike crashed Windows computers worldwide and disrupted GTA hospitals and airports. Ontario hospitals use Code Grey to signal the loss of essential infrastructure such as power, water or computer systems.
stories.headline: Microsoft says services fully restored after outage that hit Toronto hospitals
stories.impact: If your workplace, school or hospital uses Outlook, some messages sent since Thursday may arrive late, so phone for anything urgent. Hospital care in Toronto has continued, and Microsoft says there is no indication of an attack.
stories.now: The BBC reported Microsoft's statement early Saturday that the underlying problem has been dealt with; the company has apologized and has not publicly named a root cause. Unity Health, which runs St. Michael's, St. Joseph's and Providence and declared a Code Grey on Thursday, said email is back and that patient and resident care was never affected. Sunnybrook reported staff email problems but stayed open for care, and the University Health Network said patient care was not affected. Microsoft said Outlook was working again for many North American users on Friday but gave no timeline for a complete fix, and an analyst quoted by CBC expects a long backlog of delayed mail even after full restoration. The University of Toronto, Seneca Polytechnic, George Brown Polytechnic, Toronto City Hall and VIA Rail reported problems on Thursday, and Montreal's CHUM hospital network said appointment requests were affected. Microsoft has said servers unexpectedly became unavailable, that there is no sign of a cyberattack, and that it will publish a report; it has not named a root cause.

stories.summary: Microsoft said its work to fix the problem behind this week's Outlook, Teams and Copilot failure is complete and services are fully restored. The outage disrupted email at Toronto hospitals, universities, City Hall and VIA Rail on Thursday and Friday.

stories.why: The outage shows how much hospitals, schools and governments depend on one company's online services for basic communication. A long disruption slows everything from appointment notices to internal approvals.

stories.backstory: U.S.-mediated efforts to end the war stalled for months while Washington focused on Iran. Rubio said in May that the effort had stagnated. Europe has repeatedly asked to be included in any deal affecting its own security.
stories.headline: EU leaders in Dublin fail to settle who speaks for Europe in Ukraine talks
stories.impact: Peace progress could ease energy and grain prices over time. Canada, a NATO and G7 member, would feel the effects of any change in security arrangements.
stories.now: Euronews and other outlets reported that leaders at Friday's informal summit debated whether a single envoy or a team should negotiate for Europe, without settling on a person or a mandate. Luxembourg's prime minister backed Costa, who said there was no division among leaders and that the right spokesperson depends on the subject. Kallas said that under EU rules the role falls to Costa, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and herself, and that agreeing on anything else would be hard. On Thursday, U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and then briefed Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy near Dublin, where both sides said European partners would be included next time. Putin repeated Russia's opposition to foreign troops in Ukraine after any settlement, and the Abu Dhabi talks earlier in the week ended without agreement on territory or security guarantees.

Names in play include European Council President António Costa, foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Finland's President Alexander Stubb.

stories.why: A deal, or a breakdown, would shape European security and Canada's allied commitments. Disagreement between the U.S. and Europe is also a risk.

stories.backstory: Schumer, of New York, has led Senate Democrats since 2017, as majority leader from 2021 to 2025 and minority leader since. Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterms and take over in January. Schumer faced criticism within his party during the campaign, and Van Hollen broke with party leadership by endorsing El-Sayed in Michigan's Democratic primary in June. Whoever leads the majority decides which bills and nominees reach the Senate floor.
stories.headline: Sanders backs Van Hollen as Schumer keeps the lead in public endorsements
stories.impact: There is no direct effect on Ontario for now. The winner will shape how hard the Senate pushes back on tariffs against Canada when the new Congress sits in January.
stories.now: Sanders said he is supporting Van Hollen, joining Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan. Counts differ by outlet: one puts Schumer at 13 or 14 public backers, including himself, against four or five for Van Hollen, who told MS NOW that more than 10 senators have privately pledged support. Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin has declined to back Schumer but has not endorsed Van Hollen, saying she wants a concrete governing plan from any candidate. Schumer, 75, says he has the votes to stay on. The Guardian reported Friday that Van Hollen ruled out a 2028 presidential run, saying he wants to concentrate on the Senate; he had previously said he was considering one. Prediction market Kalshi put Schumer's chances at about 83% on Friday.

stories.why: The majority leader controls the Senate's agenda, including whether and when votes on tariffs, spending and oversight of the White House happen. The contest is the first test of unity for Democrats since their midterm win.

stories.backstory: OSAP is Ontario's student loan and grant program. Online programs at private career colleges became eligible during the pandemic, and spending there grew quickly: seven career colleges accounted for about $385 million in grants in 2024-25, roughly as much as all of Ontario's public colleges combined. The province barred several schools over the summer, then paused OSAP payments to all private post-secondary institutions while the accounting firm KPMG audits the sector; early findings were sent to the Ontario Provincial Police and the auditor general. Separately, thousands of students walked out on Nov. 5 over wider OSAP and tuition changes.
stories.headline: Ontario plans OSAP caps and online-program ban for private career colleges
stories.impact: Students at private career colleges in the GTA still have no date for aid to resume, and those in mostly-online programs may lose eligibility altogether. Anyone enrolling should confirm a school's OSAP status before paying fees.
stories.now: Quinn said the province found coordinated and sophisticated efforts to exploit the Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP), not just paperwork problems. The proposed law would cap growth in OSAP-funded enrolment at private institutions, make mostly-online programs ineligible, require career colleges to have a physical campus and restrict their ties to outside immigration and recruitment firms. It would also make private colleges liable for their students' loans, so the province can recover money more easily, and add new fines. The government has cited thousands of applications from the same internet address, final exams finished in about six minutes and outsiders doing students' coursework. Opposition parties dismissed it as a bill meant to protect the government that does nothing for students caught in the freeze on aid at career colleges, which began in early October and remains in place; the Liberals want funding restored at schools with no evidence of wrongdoing. Quinn has said the province is working with banks on low-interest loans for affected students until the pause is lifted in the new year.
